title: New press, same color bottleneck
excerpt: Three new offset press investments in two weeks, all promising 35 to 40 percent more capacity. The color approval loop decides how much of it you actually get.
lead: July 2026 brought a run of new sheetfed offset press announcements in North America and the UK, each with a headline productivity figure attached. Those figures are earned at running speed. The hours that decide whether you ever see them are spent before the press reaches running speed, getting the sheet to color.
paragraphs: Between 20 and 31 July 2026, three sheetfed offset investments were announced within days of each other on two continents: two Koenig & Bauer Rapida 106 presses for Prodigy Graphics in Toronto, a Heidelberg Speedmaster XL 106 for Zenith Print Group in the UK, and the first UK installation of a Komori G837P Advance EX Edition at Selsey Press. Each announcement carried a productivity claim of roughly 35 to 40 percent.

Those claims are real, and they are rated at running speed on a press that is already printing to color. As run lengths shorten, the share of press time spent running falls and the share spent changing over rises, so a rated speed gain returns less and less of itself. The constraint moves to makeready, and inside makeready it moves to color approval.

A new press shortens the mechanical part of makeready. Plate changes, blanket washes and CIP3 ink presetting are all faster than on a press from ten years ago. What it does not shorten by itself is the loop where an operator measures a sheet, judges the result and moves the ink keys by hand. That loop is manual on most installations, including brand new ones.

Closed loop color control is what automates that last step: the color bar is scanned, the software calculates the ink key correction and sends it to the console, and the operator validates instead of calculating. It applies to presses already on the floor as much as to presses on order, which is why the same conversation is happening in Toronto, in the UK, in Mexican packaging plants and in Japanese commercial shops at the same time.

body.text: Between 20 and 31 July 2026, three sheetfed offset investments were announced within days of each other, on two continents. Each came with a productivity number in the headline. Read together they say something useful about where offset is going, and about the part of the job the machine builder cannot fix for you.
What the new offset press announcements actually promise
The three announcements are close enough in format to compare directly.

items: Prodigy Graphics, a trade printer in Toronto, is installing two Koenig & Bauer Rapida 106 presses, a four color plus coater and an eight color plus coater and perfector, and expects a 40 percent increase in efficiency and capacity.
Zenith Print Group in the UK has bought a Heidelberg Speedmaster XL 106-5-P+L, quoted at roughly 35 percent additional production capacity.
Selsey Press has installed the first Komori G837P Advance EX Edition in the UK, a perfecting press bought as a multi million pound investment.

body.text: Three builders, three formats, one shared claim: more sheets per shift. That claim is real. It is also rated at running speed, on a press that is already printing to color.
Where a rated capacity gain actually gets spent

The typical commercial and packaging job has been getting shorter for a decade. When run lengths fall, the share of press time spent running falls with them, and the share spent changing over rises. A press that runs 20 percent faster on a four hour job returns most of that gain. The same press on a forty minute job returns very little of it, because the job is dominated by everything that happens before the first good sheet.
That is the arithmetic behind a lot of disappointing capex. The press meets its specification. The shop does not see the promised capacity, because the constraint moved.

items: Plate change and washup: automated on every current 106 format press, already fast, little headroom left
Ink presetting from CIP3 or CIP4 data: puts the ink zones approximately right before the first sheet
Color approval: print, measure, adjust the ink keys, print again, measure again, until the sheet is inside tolerance. This loop is manual on most presses, and it is where the remaining minutes sit

body.text: Does a new press make makeready faster?

Partly. A new press shortens the mechanical part of makeready: plate changes, blanket washes, format changes and ink presetting are all faster and more automated than on a press from ten years ago. What it does not shorten by itself is the color approval loop, because that loop depends on measuring the sheet and deciding what to change. On most installations, including brand new ones, an operator still reads a measurement, judges it and moves the ink keys by hand. The press got faster. The decision did not.
The part that does not come in the crate

CIP3 and CIP4 presetting is the standard answer here, and it is a genuinely good one. Ink zone openings are calculated from the plate image before the job starts, so the first sheet lands in the neighbourhood of the target rather than nowhere near it. Presetting is the reason makeready waste on a modern press is counted in dozens of sheets rather than hundreds.

It is also open loop. Presetting predicts, it does not verify. Paper, ink batch, temperature, humidity, blanket condition and press speed all move the result away from the prediction, and nothing in the presetting chain measures that drift or corrects it. Closing the gap between the presetting sheet and the approved sheet is still manual work, and it is still repeated at every speed change and every recovery during the run.
What is closed loop color control on an offset press?

It is the step that turns a measurement into an ink key correction automatically. The color bar is scanned, the software compares each zone against the target values, calculates the correction and sends it to the press console. The operator validates rather than calculates. Because the loop works on measured data rather than on judgement, the second sheet is closer than it would otherwise be, the third closer again, and the run holds after approval. How that loop works, the waste and makeready numbers behind it and what a retrofit involves are set out in the [complete closed loop guide](/closed-loop-color-control). The measurement side is served by an ecosystem of scanning and reporting tools, X-Rite IntelliTrax2 and MeasureColor among them, but the correction itself is what closes the loop.
Why this is a worldwide pattern, not a local one

It is worth noting where these three announcements came from: Toronto and two UK shops, inside two weeks. The same conversation is happening in packaging plants in Mexico, in commercial shops in Japan and in carton converters across Europe, because the underlying pressure is identical everywhere. Run lengths are shorter, the tolerances brand owners impose are tighter, and experienced press operators are harder to recruit than they were. Closed loop color control is running on more than 1,000 systems in over 30 countries for exactly that reason: the constraint is not regional. North American printers weighing this alongside a press order will find the local view on the [Canada page](/canada).
Does a press have to be new to run closed loop?

No. What matters is the console: whether it exposes an interface that accepts ink key corrections, and whether a measurement source is available press side. Many consoles from the previous generation qualify, including Heidelberg CP2000 and Prinect Press Center, Komori PQC-S and KHS-AI, Koenig & Bauer ErgoTronic and Manroland ColorPilot. The quickest way to settle it for a specific machine is the free [console eligibility check](/console-validation): a few photographs of the console, an answer within one business day. Terms used above, from makeready to ink zone, are defined in the [glossary](/glossary).
The number to run before the press arrives

If a press order is on the table, the useful exercise is to split the promised gain in two. Ask the builder what share of the quoted 35 or 40 percent comes from running speed, and what share comes from faster changeover. Then take your own job list and work out how many hours per week actually go into color approval, at your average run length, in your ink and substrate mix. That second number is the one a press purchase leaves largely untouched and a closed loop addresses directly. The [ROI calculator](/roi) does the arithmetic on waste sheets, makeready minutes, ink and energy if you would rather not build the spreadsheet yourself.

None of this is an argument against buying the press. A Rapida 106, an XL 106 or a G837P is a better machine than what it replaces, and the capacity is real. The point is narrower: the new press raises the ceiling, and the color approval loop sets the floor. Raising one without raising the other is how a 40 percent investment turns into a 15 percent result.

Chacun affichait un gain de productivité dans son titre. Lus ensemble, ils disent quelque chose d'utile sur la direction que prend l'offset, et sur la partie du travail que le constructeur ne peut pas régler à votre place.
Ce que promettent réellement ces nouvelles presses offset
Les trois annonces sont assez proches dans leur format pour être comparées directement.

items: Prodigy Graphics, imprimeur de labeur à Toronto, installe deux Koenig & Bauer Rapida 106, une quatre couleurs plus vernis et une huit couleurs plus vernis avec retiration, et attend 40 pour cent d'efficacité et de capacité en plus.
Zenith Print Group, au Royaume-Uni, a commandé une Heidelberg Speedmaster XL 106-5-P+L, annoncée à environ 35 pour cent de capacité de production supplémentaire.
Selsey Press a installé la première Komori G837P Advance EX Edition du Royaume-Uni, une presse à retiration achetée pour plusieurs millions de livres.

body.text: Trois constructeurs, trois formats, une promesse commune : plus de feuilles par équipe. Cette promesse est réelle. Elle est aussi mesurée en vitesse de tirage, sur une presse qui imprime déjà à la couleur.
Où part réellement un gain de capacité

Le travail type, en labeur comme en packaging, raccourcit depuis dix ans. Quand les tirages baissent, la part du temps presse passée à imprimer baisse avec eux, et la part passée à changer de travail monte. Une presse 20 pour cent plus rapide sur un travail de quatre heures restitue l'essentiel de ce gain. La même presse sur un travail de quarante minutes n'en restitue presque rien, parce que le travail est dominé par tout ce qui se passe avant la première feuille bonne.
C'est l'arithmétique qui explique beaucoup d'investissements décevants. La presse tient sa spécification. L'atelier ne voit pas la capacité promise, parce que la contrainte s'est déplacée.

items: Changement de plaques et lavage : automatisés sur toutes les presses format 106 actuelles, déjà rapides, il reste peu de marge
Préréglage d'encrage à partir des données CIP3 ou CIP4 : place les zones d'encrage approximativement avant la première feuille

Validation couleur : imprimer, mesurer, corriger les vis d'encrier, réimprimer, remesurer, jusqu'à ce que la feuille entre dans la tolérance. Cette boucle est manuelle sur la plupart des presses, et c'est là que se logent les minutes restantes

body.text: Une presse neuve accélère-t-elle le calage ?

En partie. Une presse neuve raccourcit la part mécanique du calage : changements de plaques, lavages de blanchets, changements de format et préréglage d'encrage sont tous plus rapides et plus automatisés que sur une presse de dix ans. Ce qu'elle ne raccourcit pas d'elle-même, c'est la boucle de validation couleur, parce que cette boucle dépend de la mesure de la feuille et de la décision qui suit. Sur la plupart des installations, y compris neuves, un opérateur lit encore une mesure, la juge et bouge les vis d'encrier à la main. La presse est allée plus vite. La décision, non.
La partie qui n'arrive pas dans la caisse

Le préréglage CIP3 et CIP4 est la réponse habituelle, et c'est une bonne réponse. Les ouvertures de zones d'encrage sont calculées à partir de l'image de la plaque avant le démarrage, si bien que la première feuille tombe dans le voisinage de la cible plutôt que très loin. Le préréglage est la raison pour laquelle la gâche au calage sur une presse moderne se compte en dizaines de feuilles et non en centaines.

Il reste pourtant en boucle ouverte. Le préréglage prédit, il ne vérifie pas. Papier, lot d'encre, température, hygrométrie, état des blanchets et vitesse de tirage écartent tous le résultat de la prédiction, et rien dans la chaîne de préréglage ne mesure cette dérive ni ne la corrige. Combler l'écart entre la feuille de préréglage et la feuille validée reste un travail manuel, répété à chaque changement de vitesse et à chaque reprise en cours de tirage.
Qu'est-ce que le closed loop sur une presse offset ?

C'est l'étape qui transforme automatiquement une mesure en correction de vis d'encrier. La gamme de contrôle est scannée, le logiciel compare chaque zone aux valeurs cibles, calcule la correction et l'envoie à la console de la presse. L'opérateur valide au lieu de calculer. Comme la boucle travaille sur des données mesurées et non sur une appréciation, la deuxième feuille est plus proche qu'elle ne l'aurait été, la troisième plus proche encore, et le tirage tient après la validation. Le fonctionnement de cette boucle, les chiffres de gâche et de calage associés et ce qu'implique un rétrofit sont détaillés dans le [guide complet du closed loop](/closed-loop-color-control). Le volet mesure s'appuie sur un écosystème d'outils de scan et de reporting, X-Rite IntelliTrax2 et MeasureColor notamment, mais c'est la correction qui ferme la boucle.
Pourquoi le phénomène est mondial et non local

L'origine de ces trois annonces mérite d'être notée : Toronto et deux imprimeries britanniques, en deux semaines. La même conversation a lieu dans les usines de packaging au Mexique, dans les imprimeries de labeur au Japon et chez les cartonniers européens, parce que la pression de fond est identique partout. Les tirages sont plus courts, les tolérances exigées par les marques plus serrées et les conducteurs offset expérimentés plus difficiles à recruter qu'avant. Le closed loop tourne sur plus de 1 000 systèmes dans plus de 30 pays pour cette raison précise : la contrainte n'est pas régionale. Les imprimeurs nord-américains qui étudient le sujet en parallèle d'une commande de presse trouveront la vue locale sur la [page Canada](/canada).
Faut-il une presse neuve pour passer en closed loop ?

Non. Ce qui compte, c'est la console : expose-t-elle une interface qui accepte des corrections de vis d'encrier, et dispose-t-on d'une source de mesure au pied de la presse. Beaucoup de consoles de la génération précédente sont éligibles, dont Heidelberg CP2000 et Prinect Press Center, Komori PQC-S et KHS-AI, Koenig & Bauer ErgoTronic et Manroland ColorPilot. Le moyen le plus rapide de trancher pour une machine donnée reste la [validation de console gratuite](/console-validation) : quelques photos de la console, une réponse sous un jour ouvré. Les termes employés ici, du calage à la zone d'encrage, sont définis dans le [glossaire](/glossary).
Le calcul à faire avant l'arrivée de la presse

Si une commande de presse est sur la table, l'exercice utile consiste à couper la promesse en deux. Demandez au constructeur quelle part des 35 ou 40 pour cent annoncés vient de la vitesse de tirage, et quelle part vient du changement de travail plus rapide. Prenez ensuite votre propre carnet de commandes et calculez combien d'heures par semaine partent réellement en validation couleur, à votre longueur de tirage moyenne, dans votre mélange d'encres et de supports. Ce second chiffre est celui qu'un achat de presse laisse largement intact et qu'un closed loop attaque directement. Le [calculateur de ROI](/roi) fait l'arithmétique sur la gâche, les minutes de calage, l'encre et l'énergie si vous préférez ne pas construire le tableur vous-même.

Rien de tout cela n'est un argument contre l'achat de la presse. Une Rapida 106, une XL 106 ou une G837P est une meilleure machine que celle qu'elle remplace, et la capacité annoncée est réelle. Le propos est plus étroit : la presse neuve relève le plafond, la boucle de validation couleur fixe le plancher. Relever l'un sans relever l'autre, c'est ainsi qu'un investissement à 40 pour cent finit en résultat à 15 pour cent.

title: Three things printers get wrong about PPWR recyclability
excerpt: Recyclability is not a 2030 topic, the grades are A, B and C only, and EN 18120 gives you no presumption of conformity. What the regulation actually says, two weeks before it applies.
lead: Ask around a pressroom what the PPWR requires and you will hear the same three answers, and all three are wrong. With the general application date now days away, here is what Regulation (EU) 2025/40 actually says about recyclability, and what it deliberately leaves open.

body.text: The PPWR entered into force in February 2025 and applies from 12 August 2026. In the weeks before that date, three misreadings keep coming back in conversations with packaging printers and converters. Each one leads to a different planning mistake, and each one is worth correcting before it costs a redesign cycle.
Mistake one: treating recyclability as a 2030 problem
This is the most common and the most expensive. The widespread belief is that recyclability becomes an obligation at the start of 2030, which leaves comfortable room to plan.

It does not. Article 6(1) imposes the general obligation from 12 August 2026: from that date, all packaging placed on the Union market must be recyclable. What arrives later is the graded performance layer built on top of that duty:

items: At least grade C from 1 January 2030, or 24 months after the relevant delegated acts enter into force, whichever is later
At least grade B from 1 January 2038

body.text: The distinction matters because the two dates answer different questions. 2026 answers "is this packaging recyclable at all". 2030 and 2038 answer "how well". A portfolio planned only against 2030 has already missed the first requirement.
Mistake two: talking about grades D and E
Grading systems with five letters circulate widely in industry presentations, usually with a red E for the worst performers. The regulation knows nothing of them.

The PPWR grading system has three letters: A, B and C. Packaging that does not reach at least grade C is described as technically non-recyclable and carries no letter at all. That category is what disappears from the market in 2030, and grade C follows it in 2038.

The practical consequence: if your supplier or your consultant hands you an assessment mentioning a grade D, the assessment is not built on the regulation. Ask what it is built on before you plan around it.
Mistake three: treating EN 18120 as a safe harbour

EN 18120 has been published and is emerging as the technical reference for recyclability assessment under the PPWR. Several suppliers already present conformity with it as compliance with the regulation.

It is not, at least not yet. EN 18120 has not been cited in the Official Journal of the European Union as a harmonised standard, and without that citation it carries no presumption of conformity. A company that conforms to EN 18120 is not thereby compliant with Article 6. Treat it as the best available technical reference, use it, document against it, and watch the Official Journal for a future citation. Just do not present it internally as legal cover it does not currently provide.
What is genuinely unsettled, and why the 2030 date is conditional

There is an honest gap in the framework that is worth understanding rather than glossing over. The Article 6 delegated acts that will set out the detailed design for recycling criteria and the grade methodology have not been adopted, and work on them has not begun.

That is precisely why the 2030 threshold carries its conditionality: 1 January 2030, or 24 months after those acts enter into force, whichever is later. The detailed criteria do not yet exist in binding form, so the regulation ties the graded deadline to their adoption. If you are being sold a definitive grade assessment today, ask which binding criteria it applies.

One threshold you can already work with is the recycled at scale criterion. Packaging counts as recycled at scale when the annual quantity recycled per material and packaging format category reaches 55 percent at EU level, and 30 percent for wood packaging. It is distinct from the grade: it decides whether a recycling route counts at all. A theoretically elegant recycling route that nobody actually operates at volume does not get your packaging over the line.
Where color control fits into this

Recyclability is decided by structure and materials, not by ink. But the compliance file that sits behind a Declaration of Conformity is built from production data, and production data is only as good as the process that generates it.

A press that drifts across a run produces measurements nobody can defend at an audit. A press under closed-loop control produces a continuous, timestamped record of what actually came off the machine. That is the difference between reconstructing a claim after the fact and simply exporting it.

That is the practical link between compliance and the pressroom: [closed-loop color control](/closed-loop-color-control) does not make packaging recyclable, but it makes the evidence trail behind every run credible.
What to do in the next two weeks

items: Check that your portfolio is assessed against Article 6(1) as of 12 August 2026, not only against 2030
Reject any assessment that uses grades outside A, B and C
Keep using EN 18120 as a technical reference, but do not treat it as a presumption of conformity until it is cited in the Official Journal
For each recycling route you rely on, verify it meets the recycled at scale threshold for that material and format category
Make sure your production measurement data is exportable, timestamped and traceable to a specific run

body.text: The eight free courses in the [Rutherford PPWR Academy](/academy) go through all of this in detail, in eight languages, written against the official text.
This article is a simplified summary for training purposes, not legal advice. The binding reference is the official text of Regulation (EU) 2025/40 and its implementing and delegated acts.

title: What makes a press console closed-loop ready
excerpt: Closed-loop color control retrofits onto presses that are already running. What the console actually needs to provide, brand by brand, and how to find out without a site visit.
lead: The question comes up in almost every pressroom: our press is fifteen years old, is it too late for closed-loop color control? Almost always, no. What matters is not the age of the press but what its console exposes. Here is what makes a console eligible, and what does not.

body.text: There is a persistent assumption in the industry that modern color control requires a modern press. It is an expensive assumption, because it turns a retrofit decision into a capital investment decision, and most presses that could be upgraded today get written off instead.
The reality is narrower and more encouraging: closed-loop color control needs a way to read the sheet and a way to write back to the ink keys. Everything else is integration work.
The three things a console has to provide
1. An ink-key interface that accepts corrections

This is the decisive one. The loop measures the printed sheet, calculates the correction, and has to push that correction to the ink keys. A console that can only display values, without accepting them from outside, cannot close the loop.

Most press consoles built for ink-key presetting already have this interface, because it is the same channel that CIP3 and CIP4 presetting data travels through. If your press accepts presetting data from prepress, the write path very probably exists.
2. A measurement source

The loop needs colorimetric or densitometric readings of the sheet. That can come from an inline system, from a scanning spectrophotometer on the console, or from a handheld device used at defined intervals. The tighter the measurement loop, the tighter the color control, but a scanning device on the console is enough to run a real closed loop.
3. A stable mechanical baseline

This is the one nobody mentions in a brochure. A loop corrects the ink keys; it cannot compensate for worn rollers, damaged blankets or a failing dampening system. On a press with unresolved mechanical problems, closed-loop control will faithfully chase a moving target and everyone will conclude the technology does not work.
What the major consoles look like in practice
Console generations vary, and the specific model always has to be confirmed, but here is the general picture by manufacturer:

items: Heidelberg: CP Tronic, CP2000 and Prinect Press Center generations, on Speedmaster SM and XL presses
Komori: PQC-S and KHS-AI, on Lithrone G and GL class presses
Koenig & Bauer: ErgoTronic and ColorTronic, on Rapida presses
Manroland: Pecom and ColorPilot, on Roland 700, Roland 900 and Evolution presses
Mitsubishi: IPC press consoles, on Diamond series presses
Ryobi: PCS print control consoles, on 750, 920 and 1050 series presses
Goss: Omnicon press controls, on web offset presses
Presstek: DI press controls, on Presstek DI presses

body.text: Each of these has a dedicated compatibility page with the specific questions that come up for that manufacturer: [Heidelberg](/console-validation/heidelberg), [Komori](/console-validation/komori), [Koenig & Bauer](/console-validation/koenig-bauer), [Manroland](/console-validation/manroland), [Mitsubishi](/console-validation/mitsubishi), [Ryobi](/console-validation/ryobi), [Goss](/console-validation/goss) and [Presstek](/console-validation/presstek).
What does not disqualify a press
Several things printers assume are blockers usually are not:

items: Age. A press from the 2000s with a maintained console is often a better candidate than a newer press with a closed proprietary system
Number of units. Four, five, six, eight units all work; the loop scales with the ink zones it has to drive
Existing measurement hardware. If you already own a scanning device, it can often be reused rather than replaced
Mixed brands in the same pressroom. Each press is assessed on its own console

body.text: What does disqualify one

Being straight about this saves everyone time. A press is a poor candidate when the console is fully closed with no documented interface, when the ink-key actuators are worn to the point of not holding a setting, or when the mechanical baseline is so unstable that the loop would be correcting for maintenance problems rather than color. In those cases the honest answer is to fix the press first, or to accept that this particular machine is not the right one to start with.
How to find out in a day, without a site visit

The eligibility check exists precisely because none of the above can be settled from a brochure. It runs from a phone: photographs of the console in full view, the inside of the cabinet, the ink-key row and the machine plate. Those four images are enough to identify the console generation and the interface it exposes.

The answer comes back within one business day and says whether the press qualifies for closed-loop color control on its existing measurement setup, or for a complete bundle including measurement hardware. It is free, and it commits you to nothing, including when the answer is no.
Background reading on what the loop actually does once it is installed: [closed-loop color control explained](/closed-loop-color-control).

title: Why brand colors are harder to hold than process colors
excerpt: A brand color on a large flat area is the least forgiving thing on a packaging job. Why spot color tolerances are tighter, and what actually keeps them in range across a run.
lead: On a packaging job, the element most likely to trigger a rejection is rarely the image. It is the large flat area of the brand color, the one the client recognises from across a room. Spot colors are judged by a different standard than process colors, and the reasons are worth understanding before negotiating a tolerance.

body.text: Every packaging printer knows the feeling: the images are excellent, the register is clean, the job is technically good, and the client is looking at the corporate blue on the front panel with a doubtful expression. That asymmetry is not irrational. It reflects how human vision works.
The eye compares flat areas, and forgives pictures

In a photographic image, the eye has no reference. It cannot know what that particular shade of sky was supposed to be, so a shift of one or two DeltaE passes unnoticed. In a large flat area of a known brand color, the eye has a stored reference and a clean edge to compare against. The same shift becomes visible, and next to a previous production run it becomes obvious.

This is why a single tolerance across a whole pack rarely survives contact with reality. A tolerance loose enough for the images is too loose for the flat brand area; a tolerance tight enough for the brand area is unnecessarily punishing everywhere else.
Why spot colors drift more, not less
There is a common assumption that a spot color, being a dedicated ink, should be more stable than a process build. In practice several factors work against it:

items: Large solid areas draw ink heavily and unevenly across the ink zones, which makes the ink and water balance harder to hold
A spot color is often printed at high density, where small changes in ink film thickness produce visible color change
Substrate absorption affects a solid far more visibly than it affects a screened area
Drying and set-off behaviour on heavy solids can change the measured value between the press and the pile

body.text: The result is that the element with the tightest tolerance is also the one with the most reasons to move during a run.
Tolerances that hold up in a contract
A workable specification separates what is being measured. In broad terms:

items: Brand colors on flat areas: the tightest tolerance in the job, agreed explicitly with the brand owner and measured on a defined patch, not on the artwork itself
Process solids: a moderate tolerance, since they anchor the overall appearance
Pictorial content: the widest tolerance, judged on overall appearance rather than patch measurement

body.text: Two practical points matter more than the exact numbers. First, agree the measurement condition and the instrument, because a tolerance measured differently at each end of the supply chain is not a tolerance. Second, agree whether the tolerance applies to a single sheet or to the run as a whole, because those are very different commitments.
Background on the underlying metric: [DeltaE tolerances explained](/blog/delta-e-tolerance-print-guide).
Extended gamut changes the question

For converters running many brand colors, extended gamut printing reproduces most spot colors from a fixed set of inks rather than mixing a dedicated ink per job. It removes washup time and ink inventory, and makes short runs of many SKUs far more economic.

It also shifts where the color risk lives. The brand color is now a build from several inks, so its stability depends on the stability of every one of them. Extended gamut without tight process control moves the problem rather than solving it, which is why the converters who succeed with it are usually the ones who put the measurement discipline in place first.
Holding the color once the press is running

Reaching the brand color at makeready is a solved problem for a competent operator with a good reference. Holding it for forty thousand sheets while the ink and water balance moves is the harder half, and it is where rejections come from.

This is the specific job of [closed-loop color control](/closed-loop-color-control): the sheet is measured continuously, the deviation on each ink zone is calculated, and the correction is applied to the ink keys while the press runs. On a heavy solid, where a small drift becomes visible quickly, the difference between correcting every few minutes and correcting continuously is the difference between a consistent pallet and a graded one.
The secondary benefit is the record. When a brand owner questions a delivery, a continuous measurement log of the actual run answers the question in minutes rather than defending it from memory.
Practical checklist before the next brand job

items: Agree the reference, the measurement condition and the instrument in writing, before the job
Set different tolerances for brand flats, process solids and pictorial content
State whether the tolerance applies per sheet or across the run
Confirm the press can hold the target automatically, rather than relying on interventions between sheets
Keep the measurement record with the job, not in an operator's notebook

body.text: If you are not sure whether your press can hold a spot color automatically today, the [free console check](/console-validation) answers that from a few photographs, within one business day.

title: Paper prices up: what waste really costs now
excerpt: Paper price increases in 2026 make every makeready sheet more expensive. Here is what that does to job cost, and the one lever printers still control.
lead: Graphic paper prices moved up again through spring and summer 2026, in Europe and in Asia, on top of higher ink and plate costs. For an offset printer, the paper price itself is not negotiable. The number of sheets spoiled before the color is approved is. That is where the margin of a job is now decided.
paragraphs: Paper producers raised graphic grades again in 2026. Nippon Paper announced an increase of more than 15 percent on all graphic and communication papers from July 2026 shipments, citing raw material and fuel costs. In Europe, Sappi added roughly 40 to 50 euros per ton on graphic grades in April, and Navigator lifted its uncoated woodfree range by 4 to 7 percent. Ink, varnish and plate suppliers moved in the same direction.

For an offset printer, this changes where the money is lost. Paper is already the largest single cost line on most jobs. When the substrate goes up double digits and print buyers resist passing it on, the sheets that never reach the customer become the most expensive part of production. Makeready waste is paper bought at the new price and sold at zero.

The lever is not the paper contract, it is the number of sheets it takes to reach color. A pressroom that needs 700 to 800 sheets to sign off an eight color job pays the increase 700 to 800 times per start-up. A pressroom that reaches the same target in 450 sheets pays it 450 times. Same paper price, different margin.

Closed loop color control is the industrial answer to that gap. Presetting from the prepress data puts the ink zones close to target before the press runs, spectral measurement reads the color bar on the moving sheet, and the loop corrects the press until it holds the reference. Rutherford runs that loop on more than 1,000 systems in over 30 countries, which is why a paper increase announced in Tokyo or in Helsinki lands the same way in every pressroom that has not shortened its calage.

body.text: The 2026 paper market has been a steady sequence of increases rather than one shock. Producers in Europe and Asia moved within weeks of each other, and they were not alone: ink, varnish and offset plate suppliers announced their own increases in the same window. For a printer, the combined effect is simple. Every consumable that goes into a job costs more this quarter than it did last year, and print buyers are pushing back on price rather than absorbing it.
What changed on paper prices in 2026
The announcements that matter for an offset pressroom, in the order they hit the market:

items: Sappi Europe added around 40 to 50 euros per ton on graphic grades for deliveries from April 2026, after an earlier increase on woodfree coated sheets in March.
Navigator raised its uncoated woodfree portfolio by 4 to 7 percent from early April 2026.
Nippon Paper announced more than 15 percent on all graphic and communication papers, effective on shipments from July 2026, pointing at raw material procurement and fuel costs.
Ink, varnish and plate suppliers announced increases in the same period, so the whole consumable stack moved together.

body.text: None of this is a negotiation a printer wins. Structural mill closures, energy costs and freight have tightened supply on graphic grades for years, and producers have been explicit that the graphic paper business was running below sustainable margins. The realistic planning assumption for the rest of 2026 is that paper stays expensive.
Why a paper increase lands hardest on makeready waste

Paper is typically the biggest single cost of an offset job, ahead of labour and well ahead of ink. That cost splits into two very different halves. The sheets delivered to the customer are paid for. The sheets spoiled getting to color are not. A price increase applies to both, but only one of them generates revenue.

This is why the same waste percentage hurts more this year than last. A pressroom running 6 percent gâche was already losing money on those sheets; with paper up double digits, the same 6 percent removes a larger slice of the job margin, and short runs make it worse because the fixed waste of a calage is spread over fewer saleable sheets. Job lengths have been falling for a decade, so the ratio between makeready waste and sold sheets keeps moving the wrong way.
The math on a single makeready
The arithmetic is worth doing on your own figures rather than on an average. Take one press, one typical job, and three numbers:

items: Sheets spoiled between the first pull and the approved OK sheet, per start-up.
Number of start-ups per shift, which is the multiplier that decides everything.
Cost per sheet at the new paper price, not at the price in your last quote.

body.text: One published customer figure gives the order of magnitude: on an eight color press, average makeready waste dropped from 700 to 800 sheets per job to around 450, roughly 40 percent fewer spoiled sheets. Across presetting and closed loop, a reduction near 55 percent is typical. Multiply the sheets saved by your current paper cost and by the number of start-ups per week, and the paper increase stops being an abstract industry headline. The [ROI calculator](/roi) does that calculation from your own production data.
The lever printers still control

You cannot set the price of the reel. You can set how many sheets it takes to reach the target. That is a technical problem with a known answer: preset the vis d’encrier from the prepress data so the press starts close to target, measure the color bar on the running sheet instead of pulling and eyeballing, and let the loop correct the press until it holds the reference through the whole tirage. Our [complete guide to closed loop color control](/closed-loop-color-control) walks through how the measurement and correction loop works step by step.

ColorLoop drives that correction and keeps a time stamped record of every reading, working with the measurement hardware already in the pressroom, from IntelliTrax2 scanning bars to MeasureColor process control. For sheetfed offset, the [Offset360](/offset360) bundle packages the scanning, the process control and the closed loop into one workflow. The practical result is a shorter calage: fewer sheets to color, less ink chased by hand, and a stable tirage that does not drift back and force a second correction later in the run. For the detailed method, see our guide on [how to reduce makeready waste on an offset press](/blog/reduce-makeready-waste-offset-press).
A global squeeze, not a regional one

The increases did not stop at any border. European producers moved in March and April, a Japanese producer in July, and North American printers have been absorbing their own paper and freight inflation through the same period. A packaging group producing in several countries now sees the same pressure on every site at once, which is exactly why waste reduction is being rolled out as a group programme rather than plant by plant. Closed loop travels well for that reason: it corrects to a number, so a press in France, a press at a [Japanese plant](/japan) and a press in [North America](/usa) reach the same target with the same short calage. That is what more than 1,000 systems in over 30 countries look like in practice.
How much does a paper price increase cost an offset printer?

It depends far less on the percentage than on how much paper you spoil. A 15 percent increase applies to every sheet, but only the sold sheets carry it into the invoice. If a start-up burns 700 sheets, the increase is paid 700 times with no revenue attached. Cutting sheets to color is the fastest way to reduce the exposure, because it shrinks the quantity of paper that is bought at the new price and never sold.
How do you reduce makeready waste when paper costs rise?

Start the press already close to target using ink presetting from CIP3 or CIP4 data, then measure the color bar on the running sheet and correct automatically instead of by eye. Closed loop color control combines the two, and published pressroom figures show makeready waste falling by roughly 40 to 55 percent when both are in place. The gain is per start-up, so it scales with the number of jobs per shift.
Does closed loop color control pay for itself when paper is expensive?

Faster, because the payback is expressed in sheets and each sheet now costs more. The same system that saved 250 spoiled sheets per job last year saves 250 sheets at the 2026 paper price this year, so the same technical performance returns more money. Run your own figures through the [ROI calculator](/roi) to see the payback period at your current paper cost.

fr.title: Le papier augmente : ce que la gâche coûte vraiment
fr.excerpt: Les hausses du papier en 2026 rendent chaque feuille de calage plus chère. Voici l’effet sur le coût d’un travail, et le seul levier qui reste aux imprimeurs.
fr.lead: Les prix du papier graphique ont encore augmenté au printemps et à l’été 2026, en Europe comme en Asie, en plus des encres et des plaques. Pour un imprimeur offset, le prix du papier ne se négocie pas. Le nombre de feuilles gâchées avant le bon à rouler, si. C’est là que se joue désormais la marge d’un travail.

body.text: Le marché du papier 2026 n’a pas connu un choc unique, mais une série régulière de hausses. Les producteurs européens et asiatiques ont bougé à quelques semaines d’intervalle, et ils ne sont pas seuls : les fournisseurs d’encres, de vernis et de plaques offset ont annoncé leurs propres augmentations sur la même période. Pour un imprimeur, l’effet combiné est simple. Chaque consommable qui entre dans un travail coûte plus cher ce trimestre que l’an dernier, et les donneurs d’ordres résistent à la répercussion sur les prix.
Ce qui a changé sur les prix du papier en 2026
Les annonces qui comptent pour un atelier offset, dans l’ordre où elles sont arrivées sur le marché :

items: Sappi Europe a ajouté environ 40 à 50 euros par tonne sur les qualités graphiques pour les livraisons à partir d’avril 2026, après une première hausse sur les feuilles couchées sans bois en mars.
Navigator a relevé sa gamme non couchée sans bois de 4 à 7 pour cent début avril 2026.

Nippon Paper a annoncé plus de 15 pour cent sur l’ensemble des papiers graphiques et de communication, effectif sur les expéditions à partir de juillet 2026, en invoquant l’approvisionnement en matières premières et le coût des carburants.
Les fournisseurs d’encres, de vernis et de plaques ont annoncé des hausses sur la même période : toute la chaîne des consommables a bougé ensemble.

body.text: Rien de tout cela ne se gagne en négociation. Les fermetures de machines à papier, le coût de l’énergie et le fret tendent l’offre sur les qualités graphiques depuis des années, et les producteurs disent ouvertement que cette activité tournait sous son seuil de rentabilité. L’hypothèse de travail réaliste pour la fin 2026 est que le papier restera cher.
Pourquoi une hausse du papier frappe d’abord la gâche au calage

Le papier est en général le premier poste de coût d’un travail offset, devant la main-d’œuvre et loin devant l’encre. Ce coût se partage en deux moitiés très différentes. Les feuilles livrées au client sont payées. Les feuilles gâchées pour atteindre la couleur ne le sont pas. La hausse s’applique aux deux, mais une seule génère du chiffre d’affaires.

C’est pour cela que le même pourcentage de gâche fait plus mal cette année que l’an dernier. Un atelier à 6 pour cent de gâche perdait déjà de l’argent sur ces feuilles ; avec un papier en hausse à deux chiffres, ces mêmes 6 pour cent retirent une part plus large de la marge, et les petits tirages aggravent le problème puisque la gâche fixe d’un calage se répartit sur moins de feuilles vendables. Les longueurs de tirage baissent depuis dix ans : le rapport entre gâche au calage et feuilles vendues se dégrade mécaniquement.
Le calcul sur un seul calage
Le calcul mérite d’être fait sur vos chiffres plutôt que sur une moyenne. Prenez une presse, un travail typique, et trois nombres :

items: Les feuilles gâchées entre la première épreuve et le bon à rouler, par démarrage.
Le nombre de démarrages par équipe, le multiplicateur qui décide de tout.
Le coût de la feuille au nouveau prix du papier, pas au prix de votre dernier devis.

body.text: Un chiffre client publié donne l’ordre de grandeur : sur une presse huit couleurs, la gâche moyenne au calage est passée de 700 à 800 feuilles par travail à environ 450, soit près de 40 pour cent de feuilles gâchées en moins. Avec le presetting et le closed loop combinés, une réduction proche de 55 pour cent est courante. Multipliez les feuilles économisées par votre coût papier actuel et par le nombre de démarrages hebdomadaires, et la hausse du papier cesse d’être un titre de presse abstrait. Le [calculateur de ROI](/roi) fait ce calcul à partir de vos données de production.
Le levier qui reste aux imprimeurs

Vous ne fixez pas le prix de la bobine. Vous fixez le nombre de feuilles nécessaires pour atteindre la cible. C’est un problème technique dont la réponse est connue : présélectionner les vis d’encrier à partir des données prépresse pour que la presse démarre proche de la cible, mesurer la barre de contrôle sur la feuille en marche au lieu de tirer une épreuve et de juger à l’œil, puis laisser la boucle corriger la presse jusqu’à ce qu’elle tienne la référence sur tout le tirage. Notre [guide complet du closed loop](/closed-loop-color-control) détaille pas à pas le fonctionnement de la boucle de mesure et de correction.

ColorLoop pilote cette correction et conserve un enregistrement horodaté de chaque mesure, en s’appuyant sur le matériel de mesure déjà présent dans l’atelier, des barres de scan IntelliTrax2 au contrôle de process MeasureColor. Pour l’offset feuille à feuille, le bundle [Offset360](/offset360) réunit le scan, le contrôle de process et le closed loop dans un seul workflow. Le résultat concret est un calage plus court : moins de feuilles pour atteindre la couleur, moins d’encre corrigée à la main, et un tirage stable qui ne dérive pas pour imposer une seconde correction plus tard. Pour la méthode détaillée, voyez notre guide sur [comment réduire la gâche au calage sur une presse offset](/blog/reduce-makeready-waste-offset-press).
Une pression mondiale, pas régionale

Les hausses ne se sont arrêtées à aucune frontière. Les producteurs européens ont bougé en mars et avril, un producteur japonais en juillet, et les imprimeurs nord-américains absorbent leur propre inflation papier et fret sur la même période. Un groupe packaging qui produit dans plusieurs pays subit désormais la même pression sur tous ses sites en même temps, et c’est exactement pour cela que la réduction de la gâche est déployée comme un programme groupe plutôt que site par site. Le closed loop voyage bien pour cette raison : il corrige vers un nombre, donc une presse en France, une presse dans une [usine japonaise](/japan) et une presse en [Amérique du Nord](/usa) atteignent la même cible avec le même calage court. C’est ce que représentent concrètement plus de 1 000 systèmes dans plus de 30 pays.
Combien coûte une hausse du prix du papier à un imprimeur offset ?

Cela dépend beaucoup moins du pourcentage que de la quantité de papier gâchée. Une hausse de 15 pour cent s’applique à chaque feuille, mais seules les feuilles vendues la répercutent sur la facture. Si un démarrage brûle 700 feuilles, la hausse est payée 700 fois sans aucun chiffre d’affaires en face. Réduire le nombre de feuilles pour atteindre la couleur est le moyen le plus rapide de réduire cette exposition, car cela diminue la quantité de papier acheté au nouveau prix et jamais vendu.
Comment réduire la gâche au calage quand le papier augmente ?

Démarrez la presse déjà proche de la cible grâce au presetting d’encrage issu des données CIP3 ou CIP4, puis mesurez la barre de contrôle sur la feuille en marche et corrigez automatiquement plutôt qu’à l’œil. Le closed loop combine les deux, et les chiffres publiés par les ateliers montrent une gâche au calage en baisse d’environ 40 à 55 pour cent quand les deux sont en place. Le gain est par démarrage : il croît avec le nombre de travaux par équipe.
Le closed loop est-il rentable quand le papier est cher ?

Plus vite, car le retour sur investissement s’exprime en feuilles et que chaque feuille coûte désormais plus cher. Le système qui économisait 250 feuilles gâchées par travail l’an dernier économise 250 feuilles au prix du papier 2026 cette année : la même performance technique rapporte plus d’argent. Passez vos chiffres dans le [calculateur de ROI](/roi) pour voir la durée de retour à votre coût papier actuel.

title: Multi-site color standardization
excerpt: Multi-site color standardization keeps a brand color identical from plant to plant. Here is how closed loop turns one reference into the same result in five factories.
lead: A global brand rarely prints its packaging in one place. The same carton runs in France, in the United States and in Asia, on different presses, different inks and different operators, yet the color on shelf has to look identical. Multi-site color standardization is the discipline that makes that happen, and closed loop color control is what carries the standard from one pressroom to the next.
paragraphs: When a brand owner places the same job in several plants, the biggest risk is not print quality on any single press. It is that five good pressrooms each hit a slightly different target. The blue on a carton printed in Lyon does not quite match the same blue printed in Ohio or in Guangzhou, and the difference lands on the same retail shelf. Multi-site color standardization is the set of rules, references and controls that make one brand color mean the same thing in every factory that produces it.

The reason color drifts across sites is rarely carelessness. It is that each plant has its own presses, its own inks, its own paper and its own operators, and each of those variables moves the printed color a little. Without a shared numerical reference and an automatic way to hold it, every site converges on its own local idea of correct. The fix is to make the standard live in the data, not in the eye of the best operator on each shift.

A workable multi-site standard needs three things: one agreed reference per color expressed in measurable terms, the same measurement method in every plant, and a correction loop that pulls each press back to that reference automatically. Get those three aligned and the color stops depending on which factory ran the job.

This is the model Rutherford runs on more than 1,000 systems in over 30 countries. Closed loop color control corrects every press to the same reference, logs every measurement, and gives the brand owner proof that the carton matched in Europe, in North America and in Asia. The standard travels with the job instead of stopping at the plant gate.

body.text: A brand color is a promise made to a shopper: the same red, the same blue, wherever the product appears. Keeping that promise is easy on one press in one building. It gets hard the moment the same packaging is produced in several plants, in several countries, at the same time. This is the multi-site problem, and it is one of the most common reasons a brand owner starts asking hard questions about color.
Why the same brand color drifts from plant to plant
No two pressrooms are identical. A job that looks perfect in one plant can miss in another because every local variable pushes the color a little:

items: Different press brands and generations, each with its own inking behavior.
Different ink sets and, often, different ink suppliers per region.
Different paper and board, which changes how the ink sits and dries.
Different operators, each with a slightly different idea of on target.
Different measurement habits, from the device used to the M condition set.

body.text: None of these is a mistake on its own. Added together, they mean five capable plants each settle on their own version of correct. If the only reference is a printed sample and a trained eye, the sites will never fully converge. Color drift between plants is a systems problem, not an operator problem, which is why the fix has to be systematic. Our [complete guide to closed loop color control](/closed-loop-color-control) covers how the measurement and correction loop works in detail.
What a multi-site color standard actually requires
Standardizing color across sites is less about buying identical presses and more about sharing one numerical truth. A multi-site standard rests on three pillars:

items: One reference per color, expressed as spectral or Lab values with an agreed DeltaE tolerance, not as a physical sample that fades.
One measurement method everywhere: the same geometry, the same M measurement condition, the same color bar logic in every plant.
One correction loop per press that reads each sheet and drives it back to the shared reference automatically, so the target is enforced rather than hoped for.

body.text: The first two make the sites speak the same language. The third makes them act on it in real time. A reference that lives in a spreadsheet but is not enforced on the press is just a wish. The value appears when every press in every plant is measured against the same target and corrected to it on its own.
How closed loop makes the standard portable

Closed loop color control is what turns a shared reference into a shared result. A spectral system measures the color bar on the running sheet, compares each zone to the agreed reference, computes the DeltaE and sends corrections back to the press so the color is held to the standard through the whole tirage. Because the loop corrects to a number, not to a memory, it produces the same outcome on a Heidelberg in France and a Komori in China. The ColorLoop engine drives that correction and keeps a time stamped record of every reading. For sheetfed offset, the [Offset360](/offset360) bundle packages the scanning, the process control and the closed loop into one workflow, which is a practical way to give several plants the same measurement and correction stack.

The traceability side matters as much as the correction. When every plant logs each sheet against the same reference, the brand owner can see that the job stayed inside tolerance everywhere it ran, and calage is shorter because each press reaches target faster instead of chasing it by eye. Consistent measurement also cuts gache at every site, since less paper is spoiled getting to color. The key terms here, from constance couleur to DeltaE, are defined in the [glossary](/glossary).
One reference, every region

The multi-site problem is really a global problem. Brand owners increasingly split the same work across plants in different regions to shorten supply chains and cut freight, then expect the printed color to match plant to plant regardless of where the run happened. Packaging groups that produce across several countries, like the multi-plant converters Rutherford works with, use one closed loop reference so a carton made in Europe, in North America or at an [Asian plant](/china) carries the same color. The standard lives in the shared data, which is exactly why Rutherford can deploy it on more than 1,000 systems in over 30 countries and still have every site correct to the same target. The [Obeikan multi-site rollout](/blog/obeikan-group) is one example of a group aligning color across plants this way.
How do you keep brand color consistent across multiple plants?

Give every plant the same numerical reference for each color, measure it the same way in each site, and use closed loop color control on every press to correct back to that reference automatically. Consistency then comes from the shared data and the automatic correction, not from asking each operator to match a printed sample by eye.
What is multi-site color standardization?

Multi-site color standardization is the practice of making one brand color produce the same measured result across every plant that prints it. It combines a shared reference, an identical measurement method and an automatic correction loop so that color consistency does not depend on which factory ran the job. The core terms are defined in the [glossary](/glossary).
Can different press brands hold the same color standard?

Yes. Because closed loop corrects to a numerical reference rather than to a specific machine, presses from different brands and generations can hold the same standard. ColorLoop is press agnostic and works with Heidelberg, Komori, Koenig and Bauer, Manroland and others, so a mixed fleet across several plants can still converge on one brand color.

fr.title: Standardisation couleur multi-sites
fr.excerpt: La standardisation couleur multi-sites garde une couleur de marque identique d’une usine à l’autre. Voici comment le closed loop transforme une référence unique en même résultat dans cinq usines.
fr.lead: Une marque mondiale imprime rarement son packaging au même endroit. Le même étui tourne en France, aux États-Unis et en Asie, sur des presses, des encres et des opérateurs différents, et pourtant la couleur en rayon doit paraître identique. La standardisation couleur multi-sites est la discipline qui rend cela possible, et le closed loop est ce qui transporte le standard d’un atelier à l’autre.

body.text: Une couleur de marque est une promesse faite au consommateur : le même rouge, le même bleu, où que le produit apparaisse. Tenir cette promesse est simple sur une presse, dans un bâtiment. Cela devient difficile dès que le même packaging est produit dans plusieurs usines, dans plusieurs pays, en même temps. C’est le problème multi-sites, et l’une des raisons les plus fréquentes pour lesquelles une marque commence à poser des questions difficiles sur la couleur.
Pourquoi la même couleur de marque dérive d’une usine à l’autre
Deux ateliers ne sont jamais identiques. Un travail parfait dans une usine peut manquer sa cible dans une autre, car chaque variable locale déplace un peu la couleur :

items: Des marques et générations de presses différentes, chacune avec son comportement d’encrage.
Des jeux d’encres différents et, souvent, des fournisseurs d’encre différents selon la région.
Des papiers et cartons différents, qui changent la façon dont l’encre se pose et sèche.
Des opérateurs différents, chacun avec sa propre idée du bon à rouler.
Des habitudes de mesure différentes, du dispositif utilisé à la condition M choisie.

body.text: Aucun de ces points n’est une erreur en soi. Additionnés, ils font que cinq usines compétentes s’installent chacune sur leur propre version du correct. Si la seule référence est un échantillon imprimé et un œil entraîné, les sites ne convergeront jamais totalement. La dérive couleur entre usines est un problème de système, pas d’opérateur, ce qui explique pourquoi la réponse doit être systématique. Notre [guide complet du closed loop](/closed-loop-color-control) détaille le fonctionnement de la boucle de mesure et de correction.
Ce qu’exige réellement un standard couleur multi-sites
Standardiser la couleur entre sites tient moins à l’achat de presses identiques qu’au partage d’une même vérité numérique. Un standard multi-sites repose sur trois piliers :

items: Une référence par couleur, exprimée en valeurs spectrales ou Lab avec une tolérance DeltaE convenue, pas un échantillon physique qui passe.
Une même méthode de mesure partout : la même géométrie, la même condition de mesure M, la même logique de barre de contrôle dans chaque usine.
Une boucle de correction par presse qui lit chaque feuille et la ramène automatiquement à la référence partagée, pour que la cible soit imposée et non espérée.

body.text: Les deux premiers font parler les sites la même langue. Le troisième les fait agir en temps réel. Une référence qui vit dans un tableur mais n’est pas imposée sur la presse n’est qu’un vœu. La valeur apparaît quand chaque presse, dans chaque usine, est mesurée par rapport à la même cible et corrigée vers elle d’elle-même.
Comment le closed loop rend le standard portable

Le closed loop est ce qui transforme une référence partagée en résultat partagé. Un système spectral mesure la barre de contrôle sur la feuille en cours, compare chaque zone à la référence convenue, calcule le DeltaE et renvoie les corrections à la presse pour tenir la couleur au standard pendant tout le tirage. Comme la boucle corrige vers un nombre, pas vers un souvenir, elle produit le même résultat sur une Heidelberg en France et une Komori en Chine. Le moteur ColorLoop pilote cette correction et conserve un enregistrement horodaté de chaque relevé. En offset feuille à feuille, le pack [Offset360](/offset360) réunit le scan, le contrôle de process et le closed loop dans un seul workflow, façon pratique de donner à plusieurs usines la même chaîne de mesure et de correction.

La traçabilité compte autant que la correction. Quand chaque usine enregistre chaque feuille par rapport à la même référence, la marque voit que le travail est resté dans la tolérance partout où il a tourné, et le calage est plus court car chaque presse atteint la cible plus vite au lieu de la chercher à l’œil. Une mesure cohérente réduit aussi la gâche sur chaque site, puisque moins de papier part au calage. Les termes clés, de la constance couleur au DeltaE, sont définis dans le [glossaire](/glossary).
Une référence, toutes les régions

Le problème multi-sites est en réalité un problème mondial. Les marques répartissent de plus en plus le même travail entre des usines de différentes régions pour raccourcir les chaînes d’approvisionnement et réduire le fret, puis attendent que la couleur imprimée corresponde d’une usine à l’autre, où que le tirage ait eu lieu. Les groupes de packaging qui produisent dans plusieurs pays, comme les converters multi-usines avec lesquels travaille Rutherford, utilisent une seule référence closed loop pour qu’un étui fabriqué en Europe, en Amérique du Nord ou dans une [usine asiatique](/china) porte la même couleur. Le standard vit dans la donnée partagée, ce qui explique justement pourquoi Rutherford peut le déployer sur plus de 1 000 systèmes dans plus de 30 pays tout en gardant chaque site corrigé vers la même cible. Le [déploiement multi-sites Obeikan](/blog/obeikan-group) est un exemple de groupe alignant ainsi la couleur entre usines.
Comment garder une couleur de marque constante sur plusieurs usines ?

Donnez à chaque usine la même référence numérique pour chaque couleur, mesurez-la de la même façon sur chaque site, et utilisez le closed loop sur chaque presse pour corriger automatiquement vers cette référence. La constance vient alors de la donnée partagée et de la correction automatique, pas de la demande faite à chaque opérateur d’égaler un échantillon imprimé à l’œil.
Qu’est-ce que la standardisation couleur multi-sites ?

La standardisation couleur multi-sites est la pratique consistant à faire produire à une même couleur de marque le même résultat mesuré dans chaque usine qui l’imprime. Elle combine une référence partagée, une méthode de mesure identique et une boucle de correction automatique pour que la constance couleur ne dépende pas de l’usine qui a fait le travail. Les termes essentiels sont définis dans le [glossaire](/glossary).
Des marques de presses différentes peuvent-elles tenir le même standard couleur ?

Oui. Parce que le closed loop corrige vers une référence numérique et non vers une machine précise, des presses de marques et de générations différentes peuvent tenir le même standard. ColorLoop est indépendant de la presse et fonctionne avec Heidelberg, Komori, Koenig & Bauer, Manroland et d’autres, si bien qu’un parc mixte réparti sur plusieurs usines peut converger vers une seule couleur de marque.
